translations.text: Abba Poemen said, “A brother said to Abba Paesius, ‘What should I do about my heart? It is hard.
I do not fear God.’
He said to him, ‘Go and attach yourself to a brother who fears God, and through his fear you too will come to fear God.’”
Someone asked an old man, “Why does my mind wander everywhere when I am sitting in my cell?”
The old man answered him, “Because your outward senses are sick: seeing, hearing, smelling, and speaking.
If you keep their activity pure, your inward senses will become peaceful and healthy.”
Someone else asked an old man, “Why am I restless when I am sitting in my cell?”
He answered him, “Because you have not yet considered the rest we hope for, or the punishment that is to come.
If you had considered these things firmly, even if your cell were filled with worms reaching up to your neck, you would remain among them and endure them without becoming restless.”
An old man saw someone laughing.
He said:
of the mountain deer. So too is the chosen monk amid lustful thoughts.
He also said, “Fasting is the monk’s bridle in his struggle against sin.
Anyone who casts it away is a stallion lusting after mares.”
He also said, “It is better to eat meat and drink wine than to devour your brothers’ flesh through slander.”
A jar of wine was also brought as an offering, to be distributed to the brothers, one cup to each.
One of the brothers climbed up onto the vault.
He ran off it, and immediately the vault collapsed.
They went to see what had happened because of the noise.
They found the brother lying on the ground.
They began to insult him, saying, “You are a seeker of empty glory!”
It serves you right that this happened to you.
But the old man greeted him, saying,
“Leave my son alone!
For what he did was a good thing.
As the Lord lives, this vault will not be rebuilt in my lifetime,
so that the whole world may know that a vault collapsed in Scetis because of a cup of wine.”
A brother was stirred to anger against someone.
He stood up to pray and asked to receive patience toward his brother and to get through the temptation without being disturbed.
Immediately he saw smoke coming out of his mouth.
When this happened, he stopped being angry.
Once the priest of Scetis went to the archbishop of Alexandria.
When he returned to Scetis, the brothers asked him, “How is the city?”
He said to them, “Truly, my brothers, I did not see anyone’s face except the archbishop’s alone.”
When they heard this, his words strengthened their resolve to guard themselves against letting their eyes wander.
An elder said, “The devil builds on a monk’s shortcomings. If a habit stays with him,
over a long time it gains the upper hand and becomes as powerful as a natural disposition, especially in those who are very negligent.”
Do not give your belly every food you seek for it when it craves it, especially when you are free from illness.
And do not eat what you crave.
Instead, eat what God has sent you, and thank him at all times.
We have consumed the monks’ bread and all their comforts,
but we have not done the monks’ work.
Say to yourself, “Brother, put Christ’s seal on yourself, which is humility.”
One of the elders went to another elder, who said to his disciple, “Prepare a few lentils for us.”
And he prepared them.
He said, “Soak some loaves for us,” and he soaked them.
But they continued talking about spiritual matters all day and all night.
But you are a worldly person; you cannot live in this place.
Abba Isaac said, “Our fathers and Abba Pambo used to wear ragged garments covered in patches and garments made of palm fiber.
But now you wear expensive garments.
Leave this place!
You have ruined it.”
When they were about to go to the harvest, he said to them, “I will not give you instructions again,
because you do not keep them.”
He also said, “Abba Pambo said, ‘This is how a monk should wear his clothes:
if he throws his tunic outside his cell for three days and no one considers it worth picking up,
then he may wear it.’”
Abba Cassian said, “One of the senators spoke after renouncing all his possessions.
He gave them to the poor,
but kept a little for himself, for his own needs.
He did not want to live in complete renunciation and humility of heart.
Basimus, who is among the saints, addressed these words to him,
saying, ‘You have lost your position as a senator, and you have not attained the life of a monk.’”
One of the brothers asked Abba Pistamon, “What should I do? People put pressure on me when I sell my handiwork.”
The old man answered, “Abba Sisoes and the others also sell their handiwork.
There is no harm in this.
But when you go to sell, state the price of the article just once.
If you want to take a little off its value, you decide. This is how you will find peace.”
The brother said to him, “If I have what I need, do you want me not to concern myself with handiwork?”
The old man answered, “Even if you have everything, do not give up handiwork.
Do whatever you are able to do—only without agitation.”
A brother asked Abba Serapion, “Say a word to me.”
The old man said to him, “What can I say to you?
You have taken the possessions of the poor, the widows, and the orphans and put them in the cupboard.”
For he had seen that the cupboard was full of books.
They asked the blessed Syncletica, “Is owning nothing a perfect good?”
She answered, “It is an even greater, perfect good for those who have no strength.
For those who persevere in this have suffering in the flesh, but grace in the soul.
For just as sturdy clothes are trampled on and washed, they are turned over forcefully until they become white.
This is how the soul is strengthened in poverty, which they embrace all the more under compulsion.
A brother living alone in the cells became troubled. He went to Abba Theodore of Pherme and spoke to him.
The old man said to him, “Go, humble your heart, and live with others, submitting to them.”
He went and lived with some people on the mountain. Then he returned and came to the old man.
He said, “I found no rest living with other people.”
The old man said to him, “If you found no rest alone, you will not find rest living with others either.
Why did you leave to become a monk?
Was it not so that you would endure afflictions?
Tell me, how many years has it been since you put on this monastic habit?”
He said, “It has been eight years.”
The old man said to him, “Indeed, it has been seventy years since I became a monk,
and I have not found a single day of rest. Yet you want to find rest in these eight years!”
They said of Abba Theodore and Abba Lucian of the Enaton that they spent fifty years deceiving their own thoughts, saying, “When winter passes, we will move away from this place.”
But when summer came, they would say, “When summer passes, we will move away from this place.”
This is how our fathers, whose memory is kept forever, spent all that time.
Abba Macarius the Great went to Abba Antony.
When he knocked at the door, Antony came out to him and said, “Who are you?”
He answered, “I am Macarius.”
Antony shut the door, went inside, and left him there.
But when he saw his patience, he opened the door for him.
He greeted him joyfully, saying, “I have wanted to see you for a long time, for I have heard about you.”
He welcomed him kindly and let him rest, for he had come through great hardships.
When evening came, Abba Antony soaked a few palm leaves for himself.
Abba Macarius said to him, “Give me permission to soak some for myself.”
He said, “Soak them.”
And he prepared a large bundle of palm leaves and soaked it.
They sat down and spoke about what benefits the soul.
From evening onward they wove them, and the rope went down through the window into his gateway.
At dawn the blessed Abba Anthony went in and saw the great length of Abba Macarius’s rope.
He was amazed and clasped Abba Macarius’s hands, saying, “Much power has come forth from these hands.”
Once the elder Abba Macarius went from Scetis to Terenouthis.
And he went into a small place and lay down to sleep.
Now there were some bones there.
The bitter pleasures.
These are the things concerning which rules have been laid down for us.
But if illness has made these powerless against us, the instruction is unnecessary.
But why do I say that the instruction is unnecessary?
For suffering that destroys sin has been provided like a powerful medicine that works very effectively in a sick person’s body.
And this is the great ascetic discipline: endurance in illnesses and thanksgiving through hymns sent up to God, so that we may lift our eyes to him with thanksgiving.
Let us not be as though we were standing under a burden, for we have cast away from ourselves the instruments of insatiable desire.
Instead, we see the glory of God as in a mirror through the inward eye of the heart, even if the eye of our outward body has been taken from us.
If we become deaf, let us give thanks because we have left useless listening behind us.
We have become [?].
We have those within us ready for battle against the enemy.
Even if illness has taken hold of our whole body, healing nevertheless increases all the more in the inner person.
She also said, “In the world, are not those who steal thrown into prison?
They are kept under guard so that they do not sin.
But let us imprison ourselves because of our sins, so that by the willing choice of our own judgment we may cast away from ourselves the punishments that are to come.”
When you fast, do not use illnesses as an excuse.
For others too, who do not fast, fall into these very same sufferings.
You have begun to do what is good; do not turn back.
For the enemy is challenging you.
For he defeated him through endurance.
Those who have undertaken sailing [?] a favorable wind; they spread out their sail.
Afterward, the wind blowing against them strikes them. But the sailors do not immediately abandon the ship because of the many winds that have come upon them.
Instead, they lower the sail a little and keep struggling against the storm that has come upon them as they sail.
This is also how it is with us.
If a strong wind blows against us, let us spread out the cross in place of a sail and complete the voyage without fear.
They said of the blessed virgin Sarah that she lived above the river for sixty years, but never leaned out to look at the river.
Abba Hyperechius said, “Spiritual singing and constant meditation weaken the attacks that come upon us.”
He also said, “We ought to arm ourselves before temptation comes.”
For they are coming.”
“And if they come and find us watchful, we will receive glory.”
An elder said, “When a temptation rises against someone, afflictions multiply for him on every side, so that he becomes discouraged and grumbles.”
And the elder spoke as follows:
“There was a brother in the Cells against whom a temptation arose.
Whenever anyone saw him, he would not be willing to open the door for him or bring him into his cell.
And when he needed bread, no one would give him any, even on credit.
And when he went out to the harvest, they would not invite him, not even to church, although it was [?] to invite them to the fellowship meal.
Once he came out of the desert,
and he had no bread in his cell.
Yet in all these things he kept giving thanks to God.
But God saw his endurance and removed it from him.
[?] in this way.
“I will come and live beside the water.”
When he said this, he turned his face and saw someone following him, counting the tracks left by the soles of his feet.
He asked him, “Who are you?”
He replied, “I am an angel of the Lord.
I was sent to count your footsteps and give you your reward.”
When the old man heard this, he was reassured and became even more eager.
He went another five miles farther into the desert.
The old men said, “If a temptation arises against you in the place where you are, do not abandon your place during the temptation.
Otherwise, in the place you go to, you will again find what you are fleeing from.
Instead, persevere until the temptation passes, so that your departure may be [?] a stumbling block, and at a time of peace, so that your departure may not cause distress to those [?] in the [?].”
“I will struggle against my thoughts so as not to touch her.”
Abba Abraham said to him, “So you see, you have not killed the passion. It is still alive, but it is bound.”
“Again, suppose you are walking along the road and see stones and broken pottery, with gold among them. Can your heart regard the gold as it does these other things?”
He said, “No, but I will struggle against my thoughts so as not to take it.”
The old man said to him, “You see, the passion is still alive, but it is bound.”
Abba Abraham spoke again: “Suppose you have heard about two brothers that one loves you and honors you, while the other hates you and speaks against you.
If they come to you, will you welcome them both with the same attitude?”
He said, “No, but I will struggle with my heart to do good to the one who hates me just as to the one who loves me.”
Abba Abraham said to him, “So the passions are alive, but they are bound by the holy ones.”
One of our fathers said, “There was an old man in the Cells who practiced austerities and wore a mat. He went to Abba Ammonas.
The old man saw him wearing the mat.
He said to him, ‘This will not benefit you at all.’
And he asked him, ‘Three thoughts are troubling me:
either to wander off into the desert, or to go to a foreign land where no one will know me, or to shut myself up in a cell, meet no one, and eat every other day.’
Abba Ammonas said to him, ‘None of these three will benefit you.
Instead, stay in your cell, eat a little every day, and always keep the tax collector’s words in your heart.
Then you will be able to be saved.’”
Abba Daniel said, “To the extent that the body flourishes, the soul grows weak.”
“And to the extent that the body grows weak, the soul flourishes.”
They said in Scetis about Abba Daniel that when the barbarians came, the brothers fled. But the old man said, “If God does not care for me, why am I alive?”
He passed out through the barbarians, and they did not see him. The old man said, “Look, God has taken care of me, and I have not died.”
“You too, do your part as a human being and flee like the other fathers.”
Abba Daniel said, “At the time when Abba Arsenius was in Scetis, there was a monk there who stole the old men’s belongings.”
Abba Arsenius, wishing to benefit his soul, took him into his cell and said to him, “Whatever things you want, I will give you. Just do not steal.”
And he gave him everything he needed.
He went off and stole again.
When the old men saw that he had not stopped stealing, they drove him away, saying, “If a brother is found to have a fault arising from weakness, we must support him until he becomes strong.”
“But if he steals, and they instruct him and he does not stop, he must be thrown out, because he destroys his own soul and disturbs everyone in the place.”
At the beginning of his monastic life, Abba Evagrius went to an old man and said to him, “Abba, tell me a word: how can I be saved?”
He said to him, “If you want to be saved, do not be contemptuous.”
“And if you go to someone, do not speak first, before he asks you.”
He was stunned by these words and bowed down before him, saying, “Forgive me.”
“Truly, I have read many books, but I have never known wisdom.”
And he benefited from this and went away.
Once Abba Longinus asked Abba Lucius about three thoughts, saying, “I want to live as a stranger.”
Abba Lucius said to him, “Wherever you go, if you do not control your tongue, you are not a stranger.”
He said to him again, “I want to fast for two days at a time.”
Abba Lucius said to him, “The prophet Isaiah said, ‘Even if you bend your neck like a hoop, this will not be called an acceptable fast.’”
“Instead, all the more, keep control over evil thoughts.”
He spoke again for the third time, saying, “I want to flee from people.”
He said to him, “[?]”
“If you [?] alone, you will not be able to set yourself right properly.”
up to heaven.
But now, when we gather together, we descend into slander.
And each one keeps dragging the person beside him down into the abyss.
An elder said, “If the inner person is watchful, then he can guard the outer person.
If this is not the case, let us guard our tongue against every evil with all our strength.”
He also said, “Spiritual work is necessary.
For this is why we came here.
For anyone who teaches with his mouth but does not put it into practice is in danger.”
Another of our fathers said,
“A person should establish a spiritual practice within himself.
If he devotes himself to the work of God, the enemy may approach him from time to time, but he finds no place to dwell within him.
But if he is ruled through captivity to the enemy, the Spirit of God also approaches him from time to time.
But if he makes no room for him because of his wickedness, he withdraws.”
A brother asked an elder, “Tell me a word about how I can be saved.”
He replied, “Let us work little by little with diligence, and we will be saved.”
Some monks came to Scetis from Egypt.
They saw the elders, who, because of their great hunger resulting from their ascetic discipline,
ate with difficulty, and they took offense.
When the priest learned of this, wanting to cure them,
he proclaimed to the congregation in the church, “Fast and prolong your ascetic discipline and your way of life, brothers.”
The Egyptians had come there.
The Egyptians wanted to leave,
but they held them back.
When they had fasted the first day, they were hungry.
Then they made them fast two days at a time.
Those in Scetis kept their fast for the whole week.
When the Sabbath came, the Egyptians sat down to eat with the elders.
The Egyptians ate hurriedly.
One of the elders took hold of his hand, saying, “Eat mindfully, like a monk.”
But one of them pulled his hand free, saying, “Let me go, Abba, for I am dying.”
“It has been a week since I ate hot food.”
He said to them, “If you are so utterly exhausted because you have fasted two days at a time, then why were you scandalized by the brothers who always carry out their ascetic discipline in this way?”
They repented, were strengthened in their ascetic discipline, and went away rejoicing.
A brother received the monastic habit and immediately withdrew into solitude, saying, “I am a hermit.”
When the elders heard about it, they went and helped him.
They made him go around to the brothers’ cells, repenting and saying, “Forgive me. I am not a hermit.”
“Rather, I am a sinful man and a novice.”
As we are speaking about something beneficial, [?] unrelated words in the middle.
For this very reason, he does not let him remain near him.
But if he came to ask him about a saying, he would run away from him.
At first, Abba Ammoes said to Abba Isaiah, “How do you see me?”
He said to him, “My father, I see you as an angel.”
But later he again said to him, “How do you see me?”
But he replied, “As Satan! And the kind words you say to me become like a sword piercing me.”
[?] of the brothers once put Abba John the Short to the test, because he would not allow his mind to speak about anything belonging to this world.
They said to him, “We thank God.”
“The sky has given its rain many times this year.”
“The palm trees have drunk, and they will put out shoots.”
“And the brothers will find work for their hands.”
But Abba John said to them, “This is the way of the Holy Spirit.”
“They are renewed and put out shoots in the fear of God.”
It was also said about him that he would soak enough palm fiber for two baskets for a single basket without realizing it, because his mind was absorbed in contemplation.
Abba John the Short said, “I am like a man sitting at the foot of a tree who sees many wild animals and snakes coming toward him.”
Whenever he cannot stand up to them, he hurries to climb the tree and escape.
This is my situation as I sit in my cell and see evil thoughts surrounding me.
And whenever I cannot withstand them, I hurry to take refuge at God's feet through prayer, and I am saved from the enemy.
[?] one of the elders [?].
He saw his way of life and said to him, “You do not see anything through your God.”
He said, “No.”
The priest said, “We perform only a few acts of worship,
and the mysteries are revealed to us. But you undertake such great hardships, these nights of keeping watch, these ascetic practices, and this self-denial,
and you say, ‘We have no evil thought in our hearts.’ Yet something separates you from your God, and he does not reveal his mysteries to you.”
When our fathers heard this, they were amazed and said, “It really is evil thoughts that separate us from God.”
But the brother kept giving to him and became increasingly poor.
The brother went and told one of the elders.
The elder said to him, “If you want to listen to me, do not give him anything again.
Instead, tell him, ‘My brother, when I had something, I gave it to you.
Now you, in turn, bring me whatever you earn from your work.’
And whatever he brings, accept it from him.
And wherever you know there is a stranger or a poor old man, give it to him, and urge them to pray for your brother.”
The brother went and did this.
When his brother, who was a layman, came, he spoke with him just as the old man had said. He went away grieving.
And then, on the first day, he took some edible greens from the garden and brought them to him.
His brother took them and gave them to the elders, and asked them to pray for him. He received a blessing and returned to his house.
Afterward he again brought some cooked vegetables and three loaves of bread.
The brother took them again as a blessing.
On one occasion he came and brought [?] and wine and [?].
When the brother saw this, he was amazed. He called the poor brothers and provided them with refreshments.
He said to his brother, “Do you need a little bread?”
He said, “No, my brother. For whenever I was in need and took anything from you, it was as though I were bringing fire into my house, and it would consume it.”
But during the time when I was not receiving anything from you, I prospered in everything. God blessed me.
The brother went and told the elder everything that had happened.
And the elder said, “Do you not know that a monk’s work is a fire?
Wherever it goes, it burns the place.
But he benefited even more by giving alms from the proceeds of his own labor, and he received the prayers of the saints.
This is how he will be blessed.”
An elder said, “There is someone who does many good things, and the evil one [?] a little [?] counts [?] so that he will [?] the reward for the great good things he has done.
“For once,” he said, “I was sitting in the granary beside a priest who was giving alms. A widow came to him, asking him for a little wheat.
He said to her, ‘Go and bring a measure, and I will measure it out for you.’
She brought it, but he scrutinized it, saying, ‘The measure is large,’ while shaking it with his hand.
He made the widow feel ashamed.
When the widow had gone, I said to him, ‘My father, the priest, did you give wheat to the widow?’
He said, ‘No.’
I said to him, ‘If you were giving it to her as charity, why were you so particular about the measure and made the widow feel ashamed?’”
There was an elder living in a monastery with a brother.
The elder used to give bread to everyone who came.
When the brother saw what was happening, he said to the elder, “Give me my share of the bread, and do whatever you want with your share.”
The elder divided the bread between himself and the brother, and continued giving alms from his own share.
Many people were hurrying to the elder, having heard that he gave to everyone.
God saw his eagerness and blessed his bread.
The brother ate his bread and said to the elder, “Since I have only a few more loaves, take me back so that we can share our provisions.”
The elder said to him, “I will do as you wish.”
And they pooled their provisions again.
When the time came, those in need came to receive charity.
Then one day the brother came in and saw that the bread had diminished.
A poor brother came.
The elder said, “Give him some bread.”
But he said, “There is none, Abba.”
The elder said to him, “Go inside and look.”
The brother went inside and found the bread store filled to the brim.
When he saw this, he was afraid.
He gave some to the poor brother.
And he understood the elder’s faith and virtue.
He gave glory to God.
very urgently, and I want to see the king. Take me there.”
He said to him, “I will come halfway along the road with you.”
And he said to another friend, “Take me to the king.”
He said to him, “I will come with you as far as the palace.”
He said to the other friend, “Take me to the king.”
He said to him, “I will take you to the king with confidence, and I will speak on your behalf.”
They said to him, “Explain this parable to us.”
And he said, “The first is ascetic discipline, which leads halfway along the road.
The second is self-control, which reaches up to heaven.
The third is mercy, which brings them into God’s presence with confidence.”
The elders said, “God asks nothing of novices so much as obedience.”
There was an elder who lived as a hermit and had a helper living in a village.
Once, however, the helper was late in making his usual visit to the elder.
The elder was running short of all his supplies, as well as the materials for the manual work he did in his cell.
And he was distressed because he had no work to do and no food.
And he said to his disciple, “Will you go and call the man who serves us?”
But he said, “I will do whatever you command.”
And still the old man did not dare to send the disciple.
While they continued in distress, the man who served them did not come to them.
The old man said to the brother, “Do you want to go to the village?”
The brother said, “I will do whatever you command.”
The brother was afraid to go to the village because of the temptation,
but also, so that he would not disobey his father, he agreed to go.
He said to him, “Go, and I trust God completely that [?] in every temptation.”
And he prayed and sent him away.
When he entered the village, he went into the place where the man who served them lived.
He found that the man and all his household were outside the village for a memorial observance, except for his young daughter, who was alone.
When he knocked at the door, she answered and opened it for him.
He asked for her father.
She pleaded with him and tried to pull him inside, but he would not consent.
When she took him by the arm, she overpowered him and pulled him inside.
But when he realized that she was drawing him into defilement, he sighed and cried out, “Lord, save me at this moment because of my father’s prayers!”
And when he said this, he immediately found himself on the river, on his way to the monastery.
And they brought him safely to his father.
Two brothers by birth went to a monastery.
One of them was an ascetic.
The other was very obedient.
Whenever the father told him, “Do a task,” he would do it.
[?] eat [?] first, he would [?] because of his obedience.
His ascetic brother, however, was stirred to jealousy against him.
He said to himself, “I will test this man and see whether he is obedient.”
He approached his father and said, “Send my brother with me so that we can go to this place.”
And the father let them go.
The ascetic took him along, wanting to test him, and came down to the river.
Now there were many crocodiles in that place.
And he said to him, “Go down into the river and cross over.”
So he went, and the crocodiles came and licked his body.
And they did not harm him at all.
When the ascetic saw this, he said, “Come up out of the river.”
As they were walking, they found a body lying out on the road.
And the ascetic said, “If you have something to dig with, let us cover him with earth.”
But the obedient brother said, “Let us pray over him instead. Perhaps he will rise.” [?]
[?] around with me through every street of the village. They were beating me and saying, “This monk has taken our daughter’s virginity. Beat him!”
And they beat me.
I nearly died.
Then a compassionate man said, “How long will you keep beating this monk who is a stranger?”
The man who served me was following behind me, ashamed.
For they had insulted him, saying, “Is this the hermit you vouch for? Look at what he has done!”
Then her parents said, “We will not let him go until he provides a guarantor [?] to support her.”
I spoke to the man who served me, and he stood surety for me.
I went to my cell. [?] palm ribs [?] this [?] out [?] my [?] the need [?] and do a little more work so that you can support her.
And I worked at night and at midday, sending things to her.
When the poor woman’s time came to give birth, she remained in labor and could not give birth.
They were saying, “What is this?”
But she said, “I know for certain that I slandered the hermit and lied about him. He did nothing to me. It was that young man, so-and-so.”
Then the man who served me came and said, “The woman could not give birth until she confessed, ‘The hermit has had nothing to do with me. I lied about him.’”
And look, the whole village wants to come here to repent.
When I heard these things, so that the people would not trouble me, I [?]
I came here to Scetis.
This is the reason I came here.
Once Apa Macarius was walking near the marsh, carrying some palm fronds.
And the devil met him on the road, holding a sickle.
He wanted to strike him, but he could not.
He said to him, “I suffer greatly at your hands, because I have no power over you.
For look, everything you do, I do too.
You fast on certain days,
but I do not eat at all.
You sometimes spend the night keeping watch,
but I never sleep.
There is only one thing in which you surpass me.”
Apa Macarius said, “What is it?” He replied, “Your humility.
I can never humble myself. That is why I have been unable to overcome you.”
A brother asked him, “What should I concentrate on while sitting in my cell?”
He said to him, “For now, I am like a man in a deep pit, reaching up to my neck. Filled with terror, I cry out, ‘God, have mercy on me!’”
He also said, “A brother asked Apa Allonius, ‘What is self-abasement?’
The old man said, ‘It is to place yourself below the animals and to recognize that they are not put to shame.’”
He also said, “Once, while the old men were sitting and eating, he and Apa Allonius were standing and serving.
They saw him and honored him,
but he did not answer them at all.
Someone said to him, ‘Why do you not answer the old men when they honor you?’
Apa Allonius said to him, ‘If I had answered them, you would have blamed me again, as though I had rejoiced in the honor and were accepting it for myself.’”
He also said, “The ground on which the Lord commanded sacrifices to be offered is humility of heart.”
The old man also said, “If a person keeps to his proper place, he will not be troubled.”
Abba Joseph said, “While we were sitting with Abba Poemen, he referred to Agathon as ‘Abba.’”
And we said to him, “He is a young man. Why do you call him ‘Abba’?”
Abba Poemen replied, “It is his speech that has made people call him ‘Abba.’”
They said about Abba Poemen that he never wanted to put his own words above those of any old man. Instead, he honored their words more than his own.
Once the blessed Abba Theophilus, the archbishop, went to Scetis.
The brothers gathered and said to Abba Pambo, “Say just one word to the pope so that he may benefit.”
The old man said to them, “If he does not benefit from our silence, then he will not benefit if we speak either.”
A trustworthy brother said, “Seven of us, brothers living as hermits, went to Abba Sisoes, who was living on the island of Clysma.”
We begged him to say a word to us.
He said, “Forgive me; I am an uneducated man. But I went to Abba Or and Abba Athre.”
Abba Or had been ill for eighteen years.
I bowed before them and said, “Say a word to me.”
Abba Or said to me, “What do I have to tell you? Go and do what you see.”
God does not belong to the one who is more loving, but the one who forces himself is blessed in everything.
Abba Or and Abba Athre came from the same district.
There was great peace between them throughout their time together, until they departed from the body.
For Abba Athre’s obedience was very great, and Abba Or’s humility was very great.
I spent a few days [?], observing them, and I saw something remarkable that Abba Athre did.
Someone brought them a small fish, and Abba Athre wanted to prepare it for Abba Or.
He was holding the knife and cutting the fish when Abba Or called to him, “Athre! Athre!”
Abba Athre left the knife in the middle of the fish without cutting through the rest.
He ran to him.
And I marveled at his great obedience.
Because he did not say, “Be patient until I kill the fish.”
I said to Abba Atre, “Where did you acquire this great obedience?”
He said to me, “It is not mine, but the old man’s.”
And he took me to the old man’s place, saying, “Come and see obedience.”
And he cooked the little fish.
He deliberately spoiled it and set it before the old man.
He ate without speaking.
And Abba Atre said to him, “Is it good, old man?”
He said, “It is very good.”
Afterward I brought him a little that was very good. And he said to him, “I spoiled it, old man.”
He answered, “Yes, you spoiled it a little.”
And Abba Atre said to me, “You have seen that the obedience is the old man’s.”
And I left them, and I keep what I saw as well as I can.
Abba Sisoes said these things.
One of us entreated him, saying, “Please, you too say a word to us.”
He said, “Making yourself of no account, with understanding, will fulfill all Scripture.”
Another one of us said to him, “What is living as a stranger, my father?”
He said, “It is keeping silent, and wherever you go, saying, ‘This is not my concern.’
This is living as a stranger.”
A brother went to Abba Sisoes on Abba Anthony’s mountain, and they said these words to Abba Sisoes: “Even now you have not reached Abba Anthony’s measure, Abba.”
He said to them, “How could I?
If I had even one of Abba Anthony’s thoughts, I would become entirely fire.
But I have seen a man who can barely bear his own thought alone.”
The brother asked him again, “Did Satan also trouble the people of old in this way?”
Abba Sisoes said to him, “He causes more trouble now, because his time has drawn near. That is why he is agitated.”
Some others went to him to hear a word from him.
And he said nothing to them.
But he kept saying, “Forgive me.”
When they saw his palm branches, they said to Abraham, his disciple,
“What do you do with these palm branches?”
He said, “We sell them here and there.”
The old man heard and said, “Your Sisoes eats from here and there.”
When they heard this, they benefited greatly.
And they went away rejoicing, having been strengthened by his humility.
A brother asked Abba Sisoes, “I find in myself that my mind remains with God.”
The old man said to him, “It is no great thing for your mind to remain with God.
Rather, the great thing is to see yourself as beneath every living creature.
For this also leads the way for bodily discipline.
These are the works of a humble heart.”
As for Saint Joseph, if anyone wishes to speak about him, he will say, “He was not an earthly man.
For how many trials he was put through! And in what a country—a place where there was no trace of devotion to God!
But the God of his fathers was with him and saved him from every affliction.
And now he is with his fathers in the kingdom of heaven.”
So we too have recognized our own measure.
Let us strive.
For even with all these things, we can scarcely escape God’s judgment.
An elderly hermit in the desert was deluded, and he said to himself, “I have attained virtue.”
And he prayed to God, saying, “What do I lack, so that I may do it?”
But God wanted to humble his mind.
He said to him, “Go to such-and-such an abbot, and do whatever he tells you.”
God revealed this to that abbot, saying, “Look, such-and-such a hermit is coming to you. Give him a whip and have him tend the pigs.”
The old man came and knocked at the door, and he went inside to the head of the community.
They greeted one another and sat down.
The hermit said, “What must I do to be saved?”
The abbot said to him, “Will you do what I tell you?”
He said, “Yes.” He told him, “Take this whip and tend the pigs.”
Those who knew him saw him tending the pigs.
They were saying, “Look at this great hermit! He has lost his mind, and a demon has taken hold of him. He is tending our pigs!”
But God saw his humility, because he endured people's mockery in this way.
He sent him back to his place again.
A man was possessed by a demon and was suffering terribly, foaming at the mouth.
He struck a monk, one of the elders, on the cheek.
The elder immediately turned the other cheek to him.
The demon could not withstand the burning force of humility and came out of him.
An elder said, “If a thought comes into your mind, exalting itself in pride, examine your thoughts to see whether you have kept the commandments:

whether you have loved your enemies, whether you have rejoiced at your enemies' honor and grieved over their loss, whether you regard yourself as a useless servant and a greater sinner than everyone else.
And even with these things, do not think yourself great, as though you had accomplished everything,
knowing that this thought nullifies every deed.”
An elder said, “Do not let your heart speak against your brother, saying, ‘I am more vigilant than he is,’ or, ‘I practice more self-discipline than he does,’ or, ‘I understand more than he does.’
Instead, submit to the spirit of poverty for Christ's sake, and acquire love without hypocrisy, so that you are not ruined by the spiritual pride you possess.
For it is written, ‘Let the one who stands take care not to fall.’ And be strengthened in the grace of Christ.”
An elder said, “Someone who is honored beyond what he deserves, or prides himself on it, suffers great harm.
Someone who receives no honor among people will receive honor in heaven.”
A brother asked an elder, “Is it good to make many prostrations?”
The elder said, “We see that while Joshua son of Nun was still lying on his face, God appeared to him.”
They asked an elder, “Why do the demons fight against us so fiercely?”
The elder said, “Because we have thrown away our weapons: accepting insults, humility, keeping nothing for ourselves, and endurance.”
A brother asked an elder, “If a brother brings me reports from outside, Father, do you want me to tell him, ‘Do not bring them to me’?”
The elder said to him, “Do not.”
The brother said to him, “Why?”
The elder said, “Because even we ourselves have not been able to keep this rule. We might tell our neighbor, ‘Do not do this,’ and afterward find ourselves doing it.”
The brother said to him, “What, then, should we do?”
The elder said, “If we desire silence, its example is enough for our neighbor.”
An elder was asked, “What is humility?”
He said, “It is forgiving your brother when he sins against you, before he repents.”
An elder said, “In every trial, do not blame anyone, but blame [?], saying, ‘These things are happening to me because of my sins.’”
An elder said, “I have never gone beyond my station to place myself higher than I am. And when I have been brought down and humbled, I have not been troubled.”
“My whole concern is to pray to God until he [?] me from the old self.”
A brother asked an elder, “What is humility of heart?”
The elder said to him, “It is doing good to those who do evil to you.”
The brother said to him, “If someone does not reach this level, what is he to do?”
The elder said, “Let him choose silence for himself.”
A brother asked an elder, “Speak a word to me, Father, so that I may be saved, even if you say it and we do not hold on to it, because our soil is salty soil.”
A brother asked an elder, “What does living as a stranger involve? [?]”
He said, “[?] a brother [?] and [?] a love feast takes place.”
And he sat down at the table to eat with the brothers.
But some said, “Who is this other man?”
They seized him and made him stand up, saying, “Get up and leave.”
So he got up and left.
But others were distressed, and they called him back.
Afterward someone asked him, “What went through your mind when they threw you out and then brought you back in?”
He said, “I had already decided in my heart that I am a dog: when they throw it out, it goes, and when they call it, it comes.”
The elders said, “If we are not under attack, we should humble ourselves all the more.”
For God sees our weakness and protects us.
But if we become proud, he withdraws his protection from us, and we perish.
The devil disguised himself as an angel of light.
He appeared to one of the brothers and said to him, “I am Gabriel. I have been sent to you.”
But he said to him, “Look, you have been sent to another of the brothers, for I am not worthy.”
But he immediately disappeared.
The elders said, “Even if an angel really appears to you, do not be quick to welcome him. Instead, humble yourself and say, ‘I am not worthy to see the angel. I have lived in sins.’”
They said of one of the elders that he sat in his cell, engaged in spiritual struggle.
He saw the demons appearing openly.
He mocked them.
But the devil saw that he himself had been defeated by the elder.
And he came and appeared to him, saying, “I am Christ.”
But when the elder saw him, he closed his eyes.
The devil said to him, “Why have you closed your eyes? I am Christ.”
But the elder said, “I do not want to see Christ here.”
When the devil heard this, he disappeared.
If you can stand firm while people insult you, this is greater than all the virtues.
An elder said:
“Whoever bears insult and abuse can be saved.”
They said of Abba Paphnutius that he was not quick to drink wine.
Once, while traveling, he came upon a band of robbers and found them drinking.

Their leader recognized him and knew that he did not drink wine. Seeing that he was greatly exhausted, he filled a cup with wine, holding his sword in his hand, and said to the elder, “If you do not drink, I will kill you.”
The elder understood that he wanted to carry out a commandment of God, and, wishing to benefit him, he took it and drank it.
But the leader of the robbers repented, saying, “Forgive me, my father, for causing you trouble.”
The elder said to him, “I trust in God that he will show you mercy because of this cup of wine, in this life and in the life to come.”
The chief robber said to him, “I trust in God that from now on I will do no harm to anyone.”
The elder won over the whole band because he had given up his own will for God's sake.
It was revealed to Abba Anthony in the desert: “There is someone like you in the city. He is a physician by trade,
who gives his surplus to those in need and spends the whole day saying ‘Holy, holy, holy’ with the angels.”
When the blessed Ephrem was a little boy, he saw a dream, or a revelation: a grapevine grew from his tongue.
It grew and filled the whole earth under heaven. Its fruit was very good, and all the birds of heaven came and ate its fruit.
Whatever they ate from the vine, it would produce again in greater abundance.
Abba Doulas, the disciple of Abba Bessarion, said: “We were walking beside the sea, and I became thirsty.
I said to Abba Bessarion, ‘My father, I am very thirsty.’ The old man prayed and said to me, ‘Drink from the sea.’ The water was sweet, and I drank.
I also put a little water into the flask I was carrying, saying, ‘I might become thirsty again.’ When the old man saw this, he said to me, ‘Why did you fill it with water?’ I said, ‘Forgive me,
but I might become thirsty farther on.’ The old man said to me, ‘The God who is here is also the God who is there.’”
On another occasion, another need arose for him. He prayed and crossed the river called the golden-colored
Hermus, walking on foot until he reached the other bank. I was amazed and bowed before him,
saying, “How did your feet feel as you walked on the water?” The old man said, “I felt the water coming up to my ankles, but beneath them it was solid.”
[?] saying, “I want to save my soul.”
She wore herself out trying to persuade him, but she could not prevail over him.
Afterward, she let him go.
But when he went away and became a monk, he fell into negligence and lived badly.
His mother died, and some time afterward he became gravely ill, so that he fell into a trance and was carried away to judgment.
He found his mother there among those being judged.
When she saw him, she was astonished.
She said to him, “What is this, my son? Have you too come here to be judged?
Where are those words you used to say: ‘I want to save my soul’?”
He was ashamed at what he had heard.
He stood there downcast, with no defense to offer her.
But through the providence of God, who loves humanity, [?] he recovered from the illness after seeing [?] in his [?].
This visitation had come to [?] from God. So he shut himself away alone.
Afterward he sat down, thinking about his salvation and weeping over what he had previously done in his carelessness.
Such remorse came over him that many people urged him to give himself a little rest, so that he would not collapse from so much weeping.
But he refused to be comforted, saying, “If I could not bear my mother’s reproach, how will I be able to bear the shame on the day of judgment before Christ and all his angels?”
An elder said, “If people’s souls could leave their bodies from fear after the resurrection at God’s coming, the world would die of terror and trembling.”
For what will it be like to see the heavens split apart and God reveal himself in wrath and menace,
[?] countless hosts of angels [?] for all humanity to see these things at once?
Therefore we ought to think this way, as though we were going to give an account to God every day, because we will be questioned about what we have done during our lives.
A brother asked an elder, “My father, why is my heart hard, without any fear of God in it?”
The elder said to him, “I think that if a person holds on to self-reproach in his heart, he will acquire the fear of God.”
The brother said to him, “What is self-reproach?”
The elder said, “It means that a person should reproach his soul in everything, saying to it, ‘Remember that we must meet God.’”
“He should also say, ‘What business do I have with other people?’”
“If someone persists in these things, the fear of God will come to him.”
He also said, “The monk’s lean body draws the soul up from the pits below and dries up pleasures through fasting.”
He also said, “The innocent monk is crowned on earth, and he is also crowned in heaven before God.”
He also said, “The monk who does not control his tongue, especially when angry, will never master any passion.”
He also said, “Do not let any evil word come out of your mouth, for a grapevine does not produce thorns.”
He also said, “The serpent deceived Eve until she was cast out of paradise. Anyone who slanders his brother is like the serpent.”
For he destroys the soul of the person who listens, and he does not save his own soul either.
Once there was a feast in Scetis, and an elder was given a cup of wine.
He said, “Take this death away from me.”
When the others who were eating with him saw this, they did not take any.
Abba Hyperichius said, “The monk’s treasure is to acquire no material possessions for himself.”
“Store up provisions for yourself and gather treasure for yourself in heaven, for eternal rest will be yours without end.”
There was one of the holy men called Philagrius who lived in Jerusalem. He worked hard to earn his own bread.
While a brother was standing in the marketplace selling his handiwork, he happened to find a purse containing a thousand gold coins.
He stayed where he was, saying, “The person who lost it must come.”
And sure enough, that man came, weeping.
The old man took hold of him, led him aside, and gave it to him.
The man held on to him, wanting to give him one of the coins, but the old man refused to accept it.
Then the man began shouting, “Come and see a man of God and what he has done!”
But the old man slipped away secretly and left the city so that they would not recognize him.
Abba Benjamin [?] to his disciples: “Walk along the king’s highway and count the miles, and you will not grow weary.”
Abba Bessarion said, “I spent forty nights standing in the middle of a thornbush without sleeping.”
One day one of the brothers asked him, “Abba, if something frightening happens suddenly, are you afraid too?”
The old man said to him, “Even if heaven should fall to the earth, Theodore will not be afraid.”
For he had begged the Lord to take cowardice away from him.
Abba Poemen said about Abba John the Short that he prayed to God,
and God took the struggle away from him, and he became free from anxiety.
He went and said to one of the old men, “I find myself alone and at ease, with no struggle troubling me.”
The old man said to him, “Go and plead with God for struggles to come to you.
For it is through struggles that the soul makes progress.”
And when the struggle arose against him, he did not return to praying for it to be taken away from him. Instead, he would say, “Lord, give me endurance in the struggle.”
For the four churches of Scetis were devastated because of the young boys.
The old men said,
“If you see a young boy ascending to heaven by his own will, grab his foot and pull him down from there, for it is not good for him.”
A brother said to a great old man,
“Abba, I want to find an old man after my own heart and die with him.”
The old man said to him, “You are searching well.”
But he continued, “This is the way.”
But he did not understand the elder’s intention.
When the elder saw that this was how he thought of himself, as though he had done his work well, he said to him,
“If you find an elder who suits your wishes, you want to stay with him.”
in reply, said, “Yes, certainly.”
The elder said, “Not so that you yourself will follow the elder’s wishes, but—”
It was said that seven brothers were living on the mountain of Abba Anthony.
During the date season, each one would take a turn driving the birds away.
There was an elder there who, whenever he kept watch on his appointed day, would cry out, “Away with you, evil thoughts within, and you birds outside as well!”
A brother in the cells soaked his palm leaves.
Then, when he was about to sit down to weave, his thoughts would say to him, “Go to such-and-such an elder.”
But he would think to himself, “I will go in a few days.”
Then they would say, “If he dies, what will you do?”
At the same time, he would also speak about the summer heat.
He would say to himself again, “But this is not the time.”
And again he would think to himself, “However much you pester me, there will be time.”
But he answered, “Let me finish the palm leaves, and then I will go.”
Then he would say within himself, “But the weather is good today.”
Immediately he got up and left the palm leaves soaking.
He took his sheepskin cloak and went.
There was another elder nearby who had clear spiritual sight.
When he saw him hurrying along, he called out to him, saying, “You captive, come down here!”
When he came, the elder said to him, “Return to your cell at once.”
Then the brother told him about the battle with all these thoughts that had entered his heart.
When he entered his cell, he knelt down and made a prostration.
The demon cried out in a loud voice, saying, “You have defeated us, you monks!”
And the mat beneath him became like one that fire had [?].
[?] And again they turned into smoke and went away.
He knew their activity and their wickedness.
They also said about an old man that he died in Scetis.
The brothers gathered around his bed and laid him out.
They laid him to rest and wept bitterly over him.
But immediately he opened his eyes and laughed.
Then he laughed again.
After that he went on to laugh yet again, a third time.
Immediately the brothers pleaded with him, saying, “Tell us, Father, why are we weeping so much while you are laughing?”
He answered them, “I am laughing because you are all afraid of death.
And I laughed a second time because [?]
The blessed Syncletica said, “Just as a ship cannot be held together without nails, so salvation is impossible without humility.”
Abba Hyperichius said, “Humility is a tree of life that grows upward.”
He also said, “Make yourself like the tax collector, so that you are not put to shame along with the Pharisee.
Choose for yourself also the gentleness of Moses, so that you may turn your heart into springs of water, like the rock.”
Abba Orsisius said, “If an unbaked brick is put into a foundation beside the river, it will not last a single day.
But a fired brick endures like stone.
So it is with a person whose thinking is worldly and who has not been fired in the fear of God.
If he rises to a position of authority, he falls apart.
For people like this face many temptations, especially when they live among others.
It is better for a person to recognize his own limitations and flee from the burden of authority.
But those who have been made firm through faith cannot be shaken.”
